q: The weight of a body is the force of gravity acting on it which gives its acceleration when it is falling.
e: This is the textbook definition of weight.

q: The acceleration due to gravity is represented by the symbol $g$.
e: The symbol $g$ is universally used for acceleration due to gravity.

q: In the FPS system, $g = 32 \text{ ft s}^{-2}$.
e: This is the value of acceleration due to gravity in the foot-pound-second system.

q: The attracting force of the earth acting on a body is defined as the mass of the body.
e: The attracting force of the earth acting on a body is defined as the weight of the body.

q: The gravitational force acting on the body, or the weight of the body, is found to be $W = mg$.
e: This is derived by substituting $a=g$ into Newton's second law $F=ma$.

q: Weight is a scalar and is directed toward the center of the Earth.
e: Weight is a vector and is directed toward the center of the Earth.

q: Units of weight are newton, dyne, and pound.
e: Since weight is a force, it uses the units of force.

q: Units of mass are kilogram, gram, and slug.
e: These are the standard units of mass in the MKS, CGS, and FPS systems respectively.

q: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body.
e: This is the fundamental definition of mass.

q: Mass is also a measure of inertia.
e: The mass of a body quantifies its resistance to changes in motion.

q: The mass of a body defined from the point of view of measuring inertia is called gravitational mass.
e: The mass of a body defined from the point of view of measuring inertia is called inertial mass.

q: The mass defined by $m = \frac{W}{g}$ is called gravitational mass.
e: This is the exact definition of gravitational mass provided in the text.

q: Mass and weight are two different quantities.
e: The text explicitly warns that mass should not be confused with weight.

q: Mass is a vector and always a constant.
e: Mass is a scalar and always a constant.

q: Wherever a body may be, there is no change in the value of the mass of the body.
e: Mass is constant regardless of location, unlike weight.

q: The weight of the body can change when its location is changed.
e: Because weight depends on local gravity ($W=mg$), it changes with location.

q: The value of $g$ is dependent on the properties of the body.
e: The value of $g$ is independent of the properties of the body.

q: The value of $g$ near the earth's surface is $9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ (or) $9.8 \text{ N kg}^{-1}$.
e: This is the standard accepted value for acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface.
